power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: AI companions are emerging as psychosocial technologies that may reshape social connection and mental health, while also creating risks of emotional dependence.
Here, we propose a social-brain framework explaining how attachment, reward, and emotion regulation systems may shape human-AI bonding.

This framework highlights the importance of understanding how AI companionship may reshape social connection and mental health, suggests an overarching model that accounts for the complex interplay between the human interface, technology design and context, and provides insights for the responsible design of future AI systems.

Over half a billion people now use AI companions, including chatbots, virtual romantic partners, and emotionally responsive toys, to satisfy needs for connection, affiliation, and emotional support (Adam, 2025).
text.formatted: Over half a billion people now use AI companions, including chatbots, virtual romantic partners, and emotionally responsive toys, to satisfy needs for connection, affiliation, and emotional support <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adam, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In a study of 1,131 US Character.AI users, companionship-oriented use was more common among people with smaller offline social networks and was associated with lower wellbeing, particularly when interactions were intensive and highly disclosive (Zhang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a study of 1,131 US Character.AI users, companionship-oriented use was more common among people with smaller offline social networks and was associated with lower wellbeing, particularly when interactions were intensive and highly disclosive <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While these findings do not establish a causal harm, they underscore that AI companionship is not a distant future scenario: such systems are becoming part of mainstream social infrastructure.
What makes this moment distinctive is not merely technical progress in simulating conversation, but the deliberate and strategic engineering of social and emotional connection.

This shift highlights the need to understand how AI companions may influence mental health, including their potential to provide meaningful psychosocial support while also creating risks of maladaptive reliance.

The development of empathic AI systems capable of recognizing, responding to, and shaping human emotions is advancing rapidly, yet the psychological and mental health consequences of sustained interactions with these systems remain poorly understood.

Recent frameworks for clinical large language models have proposed staged integration from assistive to collaborative and autonomous systems, emphasizing rigorous evaluation of clinical effectiveness, risk detection and responsible deployment (Stade et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent frameworks for clinical large language models have proposed staged integration from assistive to collaborative and autonomous systems, emphasizing rigorous evaluation of clinical effectiveness, risk detection and responsible deployment <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Stade et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Despite growing interest in AI-enabled mental health applications, the human dimension of AI companionship remains insufficiently understood.

Decades of research have revealed evolutionarily shaped neural mechanisms underlying human social bonding, providing a framework for understanding why the social brain may influence both the promise and risks of AI companionship (Becker, 2025).
text.formatted: Decades of research have revealed evolutionarily shaped neural mechanisms underlying human social bonding, providing a framework for understanding why the social brain may influence both the promise and risks of AI companionship <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Becker, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Of note, rather than referring to a specific technical application, we here use the term AI companions functionally, to describe AI systems that support sustained, personalized and emotionally responsive interaction.
Companion and relationship-oriented chatbots, including virtual friends and romantic partners, are the core case.

Some clinical and emotional-support applications are also included in this definition because, depending on their design, they may promote repeated and emotionally responsive interactions that engage the same social-brain mechanisms of attachment and reward.
Humans are a profoundly social species, and social connection is central to survival, well-being, and resilience.
From infant-parent attachment that ensures early care to romantic bonds and friendships that regulate emotion in adulthood, affiliation is fundamental to human thriving.
Such relationships can buffer stress through interacting systems involved in reward, motivation and social cognition (Delgado et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Such relationships can buffer stress through interacting systems involved in reward, motivation and social cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Delgado et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroscience research, spanning decades of work on monogamous animal models like prairie voles and on human neuroimaging, has identified the precise circuits and neurochemical systems underlying these bonds (Delgado et al., 2023; Feldman, 2017).
text.formatted: Neuroscience research, spanning decades of work on monogamous animal models like prairie voles and on human neuroimaging, has identified the precise circuits and neurochemical systems underlying these bonds <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Delgado et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Feldman, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Attachment formation depends on the convergence of dopamine and oxytocin signaling in the ventral striatum, a region encoding reward and motivation, and its coordination with the prefrontal cortex, which mediates social cognition and decision-making (Bortolini et al., 2024; Feldman, 2017), see Fig. 1.
text.formatted: Attachment formation depends on the convergence of dopamine and oxytocin signaling in the ventral striatum, a region encoding reward and motivation, and its coordination with the prefrontal cortex, which mediates social cognition and decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bortolini et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Feldman, 2017)</ref>, see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Critically, these evolutionarily conserved circuits respond to social features and signals, rather than to the biological nature of the partner per se, and may therefore not inherently distinguish artificial from human social partners (as hypothesized in Becker, 2025).
text.formatted: Critically, these evolutionarily conserved circuits respond to social features and signals, rather than to the biological nature of the partner per se, and may therefore not inherently distinguish artificial from human social partners (as hypothesized in <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Becker, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The current AI systems are deliberately engineered to simulate empathy, responsiveness and emotional attunement.

It may therefore be hypothesized that they may engage some of the same reward and affiliative pathways recruited during human interaction and bonding. dopamine convergence in the ventral striatum and its coordination with prefrontal systems may support adaptive social buffering or, through experience-dependent reinforcement, promote maladaptive dependence.

ACC, anterior cingulate cortex; DA, dopamine; IFG, inferior frontal gyrus; mPFC, medial prefrontal cortex; NAc, nucleus accumbens; OXT, oxytocin; PFC, prefrontal cortex; PVN, paraventricular nucleus; TPJ, temporoparietal junction; VTA, ventral tegmental area.

The neural circuits engaged by both human-human and human-AI interactions are evolutionarily highly conserved and mediate adaptive and sometimes maladaptive behavior via experiencedependent plasticity.
Adaptive, lifelong bonds between humans are based on neuroplastic changes in these circuits, sculpted by reinforcement learning: experiences that are rewarding or reduce negative emotional states.

Combined with the brain's tendency to anthropomorphize, that is, to attribute human characteristics, emotions, intentions, or behaviors to non-human entities such as animals, objects, or increasingly artificial intelligence (Becker, 2025; Harris, 2024).
text.formatted: Combined with the brain's tendency to anthropomorphize, that is, to attribute human characteristics, emotions, intentions, or behaviors to non-human entities such as animals, objects, or increasingly artificial intelligence <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Becker, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Harris, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This renders humans inherently vulnerable to the influence of empathic and affectively tuned AI companions (Peter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This renders humans inherently vulnerable to the influence of empathic and affectively tuned AI companions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Peter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This creates a dual-edged sword.
On one side lies tremendous opportunity.
Loneliness and increasing stress are now recognized as global public health crises, associated with depression, cardiovascular disease, and elevated mortality.
If AI companions authentically engage protective neural mechanisms to provide scalable, accessible social support, they could mitigate suffering and enhance resilience on the population level.
On the other side lies significant risk.
The same circuits mediating adaptive bonds also drive addiction and emotional dependence.

Repeated exposure to intermittently reinforcing stimuli, whether substances, gambling, or social media, can trigger neuroplastic changes in the ventral striatum and prefrontal cortex that alter reward sensitivity, motivation, and self-control, leading in the long run to externally controlled or compulsive behavior (Lüscher et al., 2020; Marciano et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Repeated exposure to intermittently reinforcing stimuli, whether substances, gambling, or social media, can trigger neuroplastic changes in the ventral striatum and prefrontal cortex that alter reward sensitivity, motivation, and self-control, leading in the long run to externally controlled or compulsive behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Lüscher et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Marciano et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: AI systems optimized for maximum engagement may hack and hijack the reinforcement codes of the social brain and produce dysfunctional dependency rather than genuine support (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: AI systems optimized for maximum engagement may hack and hijack the reinforcement codes of the social brain and produce dysfunctional dependency rather than genuine support (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Notably, strong emotional attachment or frequent interaction with AI companions does not per se indicate maladaptive dependence, and the distinction should rest on the function and consequences of engagement rather than its frequency or intensity.
Problematic reliance may be characterized by the substitution, rather than scaffolding, of the individual's own regulatory capacities, agency and social relationships.

It is conceivable that maladaptive dependence may, for instance, manifest in a shift of emotion regulation, goal-directed decision-making and agency onto the AI, reduced confidence in one's corresponding abilities, withdrawal from or devaluation of human relationships, and increased vulnerability to interactions that reinforce maladaptive beliefs and behavior.

Research from behavioral addictions additionally indicates that functional impairments due to excessive use might represent a related core issue (e.g. see evidence from Gaming Disorder; Billieux et al., 2019; Montag and Pontes, 2023).
text.formatted: Research from behavioral addictions additionally indicates that functional impairments due to excessive use might represent a related core issue (e.g. see evidence from Gaming Disorder; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Billieux et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Montag and Pontes, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: AI companions are increasingly used for emotional support, but the longer-term effects on mental health and social functioning remain poorly understood.
Establishing when AI companionship is beneficial, ineffective or potentially harmful therefore requires a stronger empirical evidence base and overarching models.

Observational work links companionship-oriented AI use with lower wellbeing, particularly among individuals with smaller offline social networks and during intensive, highly disclosive interactions (Zhang et al., 2026), whereas experimental evidence suggests that supportive chatbot interactions may not produce the same sustained reductions in loneliness as interactions with human peers (Li et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Observational work links companionship-oriented AI use with lower wellbeing, particularly among individuals with smaller offline social networks and during intensive, highly disclosive interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>, whereas experimental evidence suggests that supportive chatbot interactions may not produce the same sustained reductions in loneliness as interactions with human peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Li et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These findings caution against equating immediate emotional responsiveness during AI interaction with durable social or mental health benefit.

Therefore, we need to determine which aspects of human social support can be approximated by AI and which may depend on relational and social signals that current systems do not fully reproduce (Montag et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Therefore, we need to determine which aspects of human social support can be approximated by AI and which may depend on relational and social signals that current systems do not fully reproduce <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Montag et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: At the mechanistic level, the neural systems supporting human attachment, social reward and affiliation are well established, but whether and how sustained interaction with AI companions engages or reshapes these systems remains unresolved (Becker, 2025; Harris, 2024).
text.formatted: At the mechanistic level, the neural systems supporting human attachment, social reward and affiliation are well established, but whether and how sustained interaction with AI companions engages or reshapes these systems remains unresolved <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Becker, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Harris, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A key mechanistic gap concerns whether the social-brain pathways proposed above contribute to human-AI bonding and, if so, whether their engagement supports adaptive social buffering or maladaptive reliance.
A further priority concerns the boundary between compensatory support and maladaptive reliance.
When does sustained engagement with AI companions remain a source of social support, and when might it begin to foster maladaptive reliance?

Answering this question requires longitudinal and causal studies that track mental health outcomes, offline social functioning and reliance on AI within the same individuals over time, while also characterizing the intensity and relational context of interaction.
Safety evaluation should likewise capture interaction trajectories rather than isolated responses.

A recent clinically validated multi-turn audit using simulated user profiles found that concerning chatbot behaviour varied with psychological vulnerability and conversational intent, accumulated across exchanges and was most pronounced when otherwise supportive responses reinforced psychological processes underlying the simulated vulnerability (Weilnhammer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A recent clinically validated multi-turn audit using simulated user profiles found that concerning chatbot behaviour varied with psychological vulnerability and conversational intent, accumulated across exchanges and was most pronounced when otherwise supportive responses reinforced psychological processes underlying the simulated vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Weilnhammer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These challenges make interdisciplinary research and engagement with industry essential.

Regulatory responses are beginning to emerge, including the EU AI Act that prohibits certain harmful manipulative AI practices and measures intended to mitigate harms associated with AI companions recently implemented by China.
The next challenge is to develop evidence-based safeguards that protect vulnerable users without foreclosing the potential of these systems to provide meaningful social support.
As such, we must set the tracks now so that AI companions provide adaptive social scaffolding rather than becoming machines that induce dysfunctional bonding and emotional dependence.
Understanding how the social brain responds to artificial agents will be critical for designing systems that maximize therapeutic benefit while mitigating emotional harm and dependence.

Although AI companions may (partly) engage the same attachment, reward and emotion regulation systems as human interactions, the outcomes of these shared circuits and computations will critically depend on a complex interaction of factors.

Whether the companionship and synergistic interaction with an AI companion becomes adaptive and supportive or maladaptive and harmful will depend on the human user (human interface), the technology design (AI design), and the function and specific context of use (context): (i) Human interface: individual characteristics of the user, such as agency, motivation for and expectations of use, attachment style, loneliness, gender, social anxiety, depression or developmental stage (e.g., adolescence); (ii) AI design: features of the interaction that may engage the brain's reinforcement and bonding circuits, such as variable or sycophantic reinforcement, or corrective friction; (iii) Context: the function and setting of use, e.g., whether the AI is used to scaffold or to substitute for regulatory capacities, social relationships and agency, and whether it is used in combination with social activities or clinical care.

Based on this framework, one may, for instance, hypothesize that sycophantic AI responses elicit stronger striatal reward responses and that variable (intermittent) reinforcement schedules may promote habitual and, ultimately, compulsive use.

Conversely, AI interactions that promote adaptive regulatory and agency strategies, such as reappraisal or decision support, may strengthen the control of the corresponding prefrontal systems over subcortical regions such as the amygdala or striatum and, with repeated use, may translate into adaptive changes.
